title: The Spanish Inside Your English
subtitle: The Latinate inheritance, el/la, quiero, and lo as 'it' walking left

use_example.german: Lo quiero, un poco.
use_example.english: I want it, a little.

summary.takeaway: English Latin roots are a Spanish treasury — and Spanish object pronouns walk one step left: it I want.

title: Hidden Twins: Places & Colors
subtitle: Direct cognates gym: la casa, el hotel, azul, rojo, grande, pequeño

use_example.german: La casa es grande y el hotel es azul.
use_example.english: The house is big and the hotel is blue.

summary.takeaway: Spanish paints the noun first and colors it second — and adjectives in -e like grande never change for gender.

title: First Sentences Gym
subtitle: Quiero el… pattern drills: assemble simple sentences and intonation questions

use_example.german: ¿Quieres el café? — Sí, lo quiero.
use_example.english: Do you want the coffee? — Yes, I want it.

summary.takeaway: Spanish has no auxiliary 'do' — your voice melody turns any statement into a question.

title: The Register Ladder
subtitle: want→desire (desear), go in→enter (entrar), finish→terminate (terminar): formal English revealing everyday Spanish

use_example.german: Quiero terminar porque es muy importante.
use_example.english: I want to finish because it is very important.

summary.takeaway: When a casual English word hides the Spanish root, trade it for its formal Latinate synonym.

title: The -CIÓN Bridge
subtitle: Hundreds of nouns convert whole: tradición, confirmación — and every one takes la

use_example.german: Quiero la confirmación — la quiero hoy.
use_example.english: I want the confirmation — I want it today.

summary.takeaway: -ción guarantees feminine gender for over a thousand nouns without memorization.

title: -CIÓN Is Always Feminine
subtitle: la complicación, la pasión, la invitación — decoding grammatical gender straight from the suffix

use_example.german: La situación es importante y quiero la decisión.
use_example.english: The situation is important and I want the decision.

summary.takeaway: Both -ción and -sión are 100% feminine — and Spanish never doubles the letter s.

title: The Article Switch Gym
subtitle: Mixed conversion drills: switch between masculine el and feminine la with confidence

use_example.german: Quiero el café y la colección.
use_example.english: I want the coffee and the collection.

summary.takeaway: Articles in Spanish weld to their nouns — learn them as one sound unit.

title: The -ar Engine: Verbs from Nouns
subtitle: Noun → verb: confirmación → confirmar. Hundreds of infinitives, ready to use

use_example.german: Quiero confirmar la reservación y quiero invitarlo.
use_example.english: I want to confirm the reservation and I want to invite him.

summary.takeaway: Spanish verbs stack without English 'to' — and pronouns can hook right onto the infinitive's tail.

title: The Celebrar Trap
subtitle: Strip the whole -ación before -ar arrives: celebración → celebrar, not *celebratar

use_example.german: Quiero celebrar y quiero explicar.
use_example.english: I want to celebrate and I want to explain.

summary.takeaway: Strip, don't trim: remove the whole -ación before adding -ar.

title: Quiero + Infinitive Gym
subtitle: quiero visitar, quiero participar — stack verbs smoothly without English 'to'

use_example.german: Quiero preparar el café y visitar Madrid.
use_example.english: I want to prepare the coffee and visit Madrid.

summary.takeaway: The -ar ending already means 'to [verb]' — never add an extra word between quiero and the infinitive.

title: The -er & -ir Verb Bridges
subtitle: comer (edible), beber (beverage), comprender (comprehend), vivir (vivid), decidir — Spanish's other two verb classes

use_example.german: Comprendo el español y quiero vivir en Madrid.
use_example.english: I understand Spanish and I want to live in Madrid.

summary.takeaway: All three verb classes (-ar, -er, -ir) take -o for 'I', while -er and -ir share -es for 'tú'.

title: Negation: The Clean 'No'
subtitle: Spanish negation is one direct word: no quiero, no lo quiero

use_example.german: No lo quiero — no quiero nada, gracias.
use_example.english: I don't want it — I don't want anything, thank you.

summary.takeaway: Spanish negation needs zero helper verbs — place no before the entire pronoun-verb cluster.

title: Refusal Gym: no quiero nada
subtitle: Double negation in Spanish: no quiero nada and no voy nunca reinforce the refusal

use_example.german: No quiero participar y no quiero comer nada.
use_example.english: I don't want to participate and I don't want to eat anything.

summary.takeaway: In Spanish, two negatives after the verb don't cancel out — they harmonize.

title: Negating the Pronoun
subtitle: Placing no right before the walking pronoun: no lo quiero, no la quiero

use_example.german: No la quiero — no quiero comprarla hoy.
use_example.english: I don't want it — I don't want to buy it today.

summary.takeaway: Pronoun and conjugated verb form an inseparable block — no stands guard in front of both.

title: Ser & Estar: The Two Beings
subtitle: es (characteristic) vs está (state/location) — the two ways Spanish sees existence

use_example.german: El café es bueno y está caliente.
use_example.english: The coffee is good (quality) and it is hot (state).

summary.takeaway: ser = what something is (essence); estar = how or where something stands (state and location).

title: Es vs Está Gym
subtitle: Characteristic vs state discrimination: es bueno vs está caliente, está aquí vs es grande

use_example.german: Estoy aquí en Madrid y el hotel está allí.
use_example.english: I am here in Madrid and the hotel is there.

summary.takeaway: Whenever you state where a person, object, or building is located, reach for estar.

title: Description Agreement Gym
subtitle: Matching adjective endings to gender: el pastel es bueno, la tradición es buena

use_example.german: El pastel es bueno y la tradición es buena.
use_example.english: The cake is good and the tradition is good.

summary.takeaway: Adjectives in -o switch to -a for feminine nouns; adjectives in -e already fit both.

title: Chameleon Adjectives: listo, aburrido & rico
subtitle: How ser vs estar flips adjective meaning: es listo (clever) vs está listo (ready), es aburrido (boring) vs está aburrido (bored), es rico (rich) vs está rico (delicious)

use_example.german: Estoy listo y el pastel está muy rico.
use_example.english: I am ready and the cake is delicious.

summary.takeaway: Where English uses -ing vs -ed ('boring' vs 'bored'), Spanish uses es aburrido vs está aburrido!

title: The -dad & -mente Bridges
subtitle: Quality nouns in -dad and adverbs in -mente: universidad, exactamente

use_example.german: La universidad es grande y comprendo perfectamente.
use_example.english: The university is big and I understand perfectly.

summary.takeaway: Every -dad/-tad noun takes la — and -mente always attaches to the feminine adjective form.

title: The -dad Feminine Squad
subtitle: -ty → -dad: ciudad, realidad, verdad — 100% feminine nouns decoded instantly

use_example.german: La ciudad es hermosa y la libertad es muy importante.
use_example.english: The city is beautiful and freedom is very important.

summary.takeaway: -dad and -tad nouns are always feminine — and abstract subjects wear their article (la libertad).

title: The -mente Adverb Factory
subtitle: -ly → feminine adjective + -mente: naturalmente, perfectamente, rápidamente

use_example.german: Lo comprendo perfectamente y hablo fácilmente.
use_example.english: I understand it perfectly and I speak easily.

summary.takeaway: Adjectives in -o flip to -a before -mente; invariable adjectives glue directly; tildes always survive.

title: Questions: Inverted & Intonation
subtitle: Inverted question marks ¿?, question words with accents, and por qué vs porque

use_example.german: ¿Por qué estás aquí? — Porque quiero hablar.
use_example.english: Why are you here? — Because I want to talk.

summary.takeaway: Every question word wears an accent mark — and ¿por qué? (two words) answers with porque (one word).

title: dónde, qué & quién
subtitle: The accented question words: ¿dónde está?, ¿qué quieres?, ¿quién es?, ¿cuándo?, ¿cuánto?

use_example.german: ¿Dónde está la estación y cuál es el problema?
use_example.english: Where is the station and what is the problem?

summary.takeaway: Pair ¿dónde? with está (location) and ¿quién? / ¿cuál? with es (identity).

title: por qué vs porque
subtitle: Asking why (por qué, two words accented) vs answering because (porque, one word)

use_example.german: ¿Por qué no quieres ir? — Porque no es posible hoy.
use_example.english: Why don't you want to go? — Because it is not possible today.

summary.takeaway: Two words with an accent ask the question (¿por qué?); one welded word gives the reason (porque).

title: The -ico & -al Bridges
subtitle: Adjectives in -ico with mandatory tildes, and invariable -al cognates

use_example.german: Es un hotel central y fantástico.
use_example.english: It is a central and fantastic hotel.

summary.takeaway: Every -ico/-ica word wears a written tilde; every -al word is gender-invariable in the singular.

title: The Esdrújula Accent Gym
subtitle: mágico, público, básico, económico, clásico — the accent mark tells your voice where to jump

use_example.german: Es un libro clásico y la música es mágica.
use_example.english: It is a classic book and the music is magical.

summary.takeaway: Whenever a Spanish word ends in -ico or -ica, the syllable right before it wears a written accent mark.

title: The -al Invariable Passport
subtitle: natural, central, formal, personal, internacional — adjectives that never change for gender in the singular

use_example.german: Es un tren internacional y una tradición cultural.
use_example.english: It is an international train and a cultural tradition.

summary.takeaway: Spanish -al adjectives match English spelling and fit both masculine and feminine nouns.

title: tú & usted: The T-V Line
subtitle: Informal tú vs polite usted (worn-down Vuestra Merced), greetings and social register

use_example.german: Buenos días, señora, ¿cómo está usted?
use_example.english: Good morning, madam, how are you?

summary.takeaway: Drop the final -s from the tú verb (estás → está, quieres → quiere) to speak politely with usted.

title: Addressing with Respect
subtitle: Using 3rd-person verbs with usted: ¿cómo está usted? vs ¿cómo estás?

use_example.german: ¿Qué desea usted, señor? — Quiero un café, por favor.
use_example.english: What would you like, sir? — I want a coffee, please.

summary.takeaway: tú keeps the -s (estás, quieres); usted drops the -s (está, quiere).

title: The Politeness Toolkit
subtitle: por favor, muchas gracias, buenos días, señor/señora — social courtesies in context

use_example.german: Buenos días, señora — un café, por favor. ¡Muchas gracias!
use_example.english: Good morning, madam — a coffee, please. Thank you very much!

summary.takeaway: el día is masculine (buenos días); la tarde, la noche, and las gracias are feminine (buenas tardes, muchas gracias).

title: tener & hay
subtitle: Possession with tener ('to hold') and existence with hay ('there is/are')

use_example.german: No tengo tiempo hoy porque hay un problema.
use_example.english: I don't have time today because there is a problem.

summary.takeaway: Personal possession uses tener; general existence ('there is / there are') uses invariable hay.

title: tengo & tienes Gym
subtitle: Irregular first person tengo and stem-changing tienes/tiene/tenemos/tienen in possession drills

use_example.german: Tengo el billete y tenemos una reservación.
use_example.english: I have the ticket and we have a reservation.

summary.takeaway: Stem vowels only split when stressed: tienes, tiene, tienen vs unstressed tenemos.

title: hay: The Universal Existence
subtitle: hay un problema, ¿hay café?, no hay nada — existence independent of number

use_example.german: ¿Hay café? — No, no hay nada aquí.
use_example.english: Is there coffee? — No, there is nothing here.

summary.takeaway: Use estar for the location of a specific thing (El café está aquí) and hay for general existence (Hay café aquí).

title: Boot Verbs: e→ie, o→ue & e→i Under Stress
subtitle: Why querer (quiero/queremos), poder (puedo/podemos), tener (tienes/tenemos), and pedir (pido/pedimos) split their stem vowel only when stressed

use_example.german: Puedo ir hoy, pero prefiero ir mañana.
use_example.english: I can go today, but I prefer to go tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: Stressed stem = split vowel (quiero, puedo, pido); stressed nosotros ending = single vowel (queremos, podemos, pedimos).

title: Adjective Agreement
subtitle: Descriptive adjectives following the noun: -o/-a/-os/-as patterns

use_example.german: Tengo un libro nuevo y vivo en una casa blanca.
use_example.english: I have a new book and I live in a white house.

summary.takeaway: Vowel-ending words add -s in the plural (libros, casas); consonant-ending words add -es (hoteles, azules).

title: Noun-First Word Order
subtitle: el libro rojo, la casa blanca — painting the object before coloring it

use_example.german: Quiero el libro rojo y la mesa blanca.
use_example.english: I want the red book and the white table.

summary.takeaway: Always name the noun before its color in Spanish.

title: Plural Concord Drills
subtitle: los hoteles grandes, las ciudades hermosas — concord across number and gender

use_example.german: Las ciudades son hermosas y los hoteles son grandes.
use_example.english: The cities are beautiful and the hotels are big.

summary.takeaway: In Spanish, plurality is a chord played across article, noun, verb, and adjective together.

title: Diminutives & Augmentatives: -ito, -illo & -ón
subtitle: From poquito and cafecito (-ito) to word-builders bocadillo ('sandwich' < bocado), pesadilla ('nightmare' < pesado), and limón (< lima)

use_example.german: Quiero un bocadillo de queso y un poquito de agua con limón.
use_example.english: I want a cheese sandwich and a little bit of water with lemon.

summary.takeaway: Spanish diminutives (-ito, -illo) and augmentatives (-ón) express both social warmth and vivid word creation.

title: The Near Future: ir a
subtitle: voy a + infinitive — express future plans without learning a new tense

use_example.german: Mañana voy a visitar Madrid y vamos a celebrar.
use_example.english: Tomorrow I am going to visit Madrid and we are going to celebrate.

summary.takeaway: voy a + infinitive turns every verb you decode into a future tense immediately.

title: voy, vas, va Drills
subtitle: Conjugating ir (voy, vas, va, vamos, van) and attaching newly converted -ar verbs: voy a visitar

use_example.german: Vamos al restaurante porque voy a organizar la cena.
use_example.english: We are going to the restaurant because I am going to organize dinner.

summary.takeaway: a + el always contracts to al; a + la stays a la.

title: Near Future in Conversation
subtitle: Talking about today and tomorrow: mañana voy a organizar, hoy vamos a celebrar

use_example.german: Hoy voy a terminar y mañana vamos a celebrar.
use_example.english: Today I am going to finish and tomorrow we are going to celebrate.

summary.takeaway: hoy has a silent H (from Latin hodiē); mañana serves as both 'tomorrow' and 'morning'.

title: Pronoun Hook vs Left-Walk: lo quiero vs quiero verlo
subtitle: Why Spanish lets object pronouns either walk left of the conjugated verb (Lo quiero ver) or hook onto the tail of the infinitive (Quiero verlo, Voy a comprarlo)

use_example.german: Voy a comprarlo hoy — sí, lo voy a comprar.
use_example.english: I am going to buy it today — yes, I am going to buy it.

summary.takeaway: Front of the train (Lo voy a ver) or hooked to the caboose (Voy a verlo) — never between the cars!

title: por vs para
subtitle: Cause/exchange (por) vs goal/destination (para) — resolving the classic struggle

use_example.german: Gracias por el regalo — es para mi madre.
use_example.english: Thanks for the gift — it is for my mother.

summary.takeaway: para = forward arrow toward recipient, destination, deadline, or goal; por = cause, exchange, or path through.

title: para: The Arrow
subtitle: Destination, deadline, recipient, goal: un regalo para ti, para mañana, para comprender

use_example.german: Es un regalo para mi madre y la confirmación es para mañana.
use_example.english: It is a gift for my mother and the confirmation is for tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: Whenever 'to + verb' in English can be expanded to 'in order to + verb', use para + infinitive.

title: por: The Motive and Path
subtitle: Because of, in exchange for, through: gracias por la invitación, por la mañana, por aquí

use_example.german: Muchas gracias por la invitación — voy por la mañana.
use_example.english: Thank you very much for the invitation — I am going in the morning.

summary.takeaway: por = because of, in exchange for, through/around (por aquí), and during parts of the day (por la mañana).

title: Possessives Agree with the Thing
subtitle: mi, tu, su, mis, tus, sus — possessives agree with the possession, not the owner

use_example.german: Mi padre, mi madre y mis hermanos viven en nuestra casa.
use_example.english: My father, my mother, and my siblings live in our house.

summary.takeaway: mi, tu, and su care only whether the possession is singular or plural; nuestro cares about gender too.

title: Singular vs Plural Possessions
subtitle: mi amigo vs mis amigos, su libro vs sus libros, nuestro/nuestra

use_example.german: Mis padres están en nuestra casa con mis amigos.
use_example.english: My parents are in our house with my friends.

summary.takeaway: Plural noun = plural possessive (mis, tus, sus, nuestros, nuestras).

title: Disambiguating su
subtitle: Why su hermano means 'his, her, your (usted), or their brother' and how Spanish clarifies it

use_example.german: ¿Tiene usted su billete y sus llaves?
use_example.english: Do you (formal) have your ticket and your keys?

summary.takeaway: One house owned by ten people is still singular su casa; ten books owned by one person is plural sus libros!

title: Three Distances of Space: este, ese & aquel
subtitle: Matching Spanish's three spatial zones to the three persons: aquí/este (near me), ahí/ese (near you), allí/aquel (over yonder)

use_example.german: Quiero este libro aquí, ese café y aquella mesa allí.
use_example.english: I want this book here, that coffee (near you), and that table way over there.

summary.takeaway: Masculine singular before a noun is este/ese (plural estos/esos); esto and eso are only for unnamed ideas!

title: Numbers & Ages: 1–100
subtitle: Counting, prices, and expressing age as possession: tengo treinta años

use_example.german: ¿Cuántos años tienes? — Tengo treinta años.
use_example.english: How old are you? — I am thirty years old.

summary.takeaway: In Spanish you are not 'years old' — you HAVE years (Tengo X años).

title: Numbers 1 to 30
subtitle: uno, dos, tres to treinta: foundational counting and diphthong twins siete (7), nueve (9), diez (10)

use_example.german: Tengo dos libros y necesito cinco minutos, por favor.
use_example.english: I have two books and I need five minutes, please.

summary.takeaway: uno becomes un before masculine nouns and una before feminine nouns.

title: Age as Possession
subtitle: Why Spanish says 'I have years': tener with age (tengo treinta años) and numbers 30–100

use_example.german: Tengo treinta y dos años y mi hermano tiene veinte años.
use_example.english: I am thirty-two years old and my brother is twenty.

summary.takeaway: Never drop años when stating someone's age in conversation: Tengo treinta años.

title: Tener Expressions: hambre, sed & razón
subtitle: Possessing physical states with tener: tener hambre (f-→h- famine), tener sed, tener frío/calor, and tener razón ('to be right')

use_example.german: Tienes razón — tengo mucha hambre y mucha sed.
use_example.english: You are right — I am very hungry and very thirsty.

summary.takeaway: Because hambre, sed, frío, and razón are nouns, pair them with tener and intensify them with mucho/mucha (never muy)!

title: Days, Months & Dates
subtitle: lunes, martes, en enero — calendar vocabulary and scheduling meetings

use_example.german: El lunes voy a Madrid y el viernes vamos a celebrar.
use_example.english: On Monday I am going to Madrid and on Friday we are going to celebrate.

summary.takeaway: Days of the week take el ('on Monday') and los ('on Mondays') — never *en lunes!

title: The Days of the Planets
subtitle: lunes (Moon), martes (Mars), miércoles (Mercury), jueves (Jove), viernes (Venus), sábado, domingo

use_example.german: Hoy es jueves y mañana es viernes.
use_example.english: Today is Thursday and tomorrow is Friday.

summary.takeaway: Hoy es lunes ('Today is Monday', no article) vs El lunes voy ('On Monday I go', with el).

title: Dates & Appointments
subtitle: el lunes ('on Monday'), los lunes ('on Mondays'), en enero, el cinco de mayo

use_example.german: Voy a visitar Madrid en enero — el diez de enero.
use_example.english: I am going to visit Madrid in January — on January 10th.

summary.takeaway: el [number] de [month] gives you every calendar date in Spanish.

title: The -ado / -ido Past
subtitle: Pretérito perfecto with haber: he confirmado, he comido — the English -ed cousin

use_example.german: Hoy he hablado con María y hemos comido en el restaurante.
use_example.english: Today I have spoken with María and we have eaten at the restaurant.

summary.takeaway: tener possesses things (Tengo café); haber launches past participles (He comido) — and the two words never split!

title: Forming Participles
subtitle: -ar → -ado (hablado), -er/-ir → -ido (comido, vivido), plus irregulars hecho (fact) and visto (vista)

use_example.german: Lo he hecho hoy y ya he visto la casa.
use_example.english: I have done it today and I have already seen the house.

summary.takeaway: hecho = Latin factum (f→h, ct→ch); visto = vista — and participles after haber never change ending.

title: The haber Auxiliary
subtitle: he, has, ha, hemos, han + invariable participle: describing recent and life experiences

use_example.german: Nunca he visto eso, pero hoy lo hemos hecho.
use_example.english: I have never seen that, but today we have done it.

summary.takeaway: Keep haber + participle welded together — place no, nunca, and pronouns in front of haber.

title: The Preterite: The Dot in Time
subtitle: hablé, comí, fue — completed single past events bounded in time

use_example.german: Ayer hablé con mi amigo y comí en el restaurante.
use_example.english: Yesterday I spoke with my friend and ate at the restaurant.

summary.takeaway: In the preterite, the written accent on -é, -ó, -í, -ió is the engine of the past tense.

title: -ar Preterite Endings
subtitle: hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron: how the stress mark separates hablo ('I speak') from habló ('he spoke')

use_example.german: Ayer hablé con mi amigo y confirmamos la reservación.
use_example.english: Yesterday I spoke with my friend and we confirmed the reservation.

summary.takeaway: 1st person -é and 3rd person -ó always wear an acute accent in regular -ar preterites.

title: The Famous Irregulars
subtitle: fui/fue (shared by ser and ir!), hice/hizo (hacer), tuve/tuvo (tener) in past narratives

use_example.german: Ayer fue a Madrid y la visita fue un éxito.
use_example.english: Yesterday he/she went to Madrid and the visit was a success.

summary.takeaway: ser and ir share the exact same preterite (fui, fuiste, fue) — 'a + place' tells you it means 'went'!

title: The Imperfect: The Storytelling Past
subtitle: hablaba, comía, era, estaba — ongoing background action, descriptions, and past habits

use_example.german: La casa era grande, el café estaba caliente y hablé con mi amigo.
use_example.english: The house was big, the coffee was hot, and I spoke with my friend.

summary.takeaway: -aba (all -ar verbs, including estaba) and era paint the ongoing past canvas; hablé and fue mark the events.

title: -aba and -ía Paradigms
subtitle: The rhythmic endings of memory: hablaba (-ar) and comía/vivía (-er/-ir), plus era (ser)

use_example.german: Yo hablaba español todos los días y estaba muy contento.
use_example.english: I used to speak Spanish every day and I was very happy.

summary.takeaway: Where English needs three words ('used to speak' or 'was speaking'), Spanish uses one: hablaba.

title: Setting the Scene: Preterite vs Imperfect
subtitle: The background canvas (estaba, vivía, era) interrupted by the event dot (llegó, vi, fue)

use_example.german: Estaba en Madrid, la ciudad era hermosa y fue un viaje fantástico.
use_example.english: I was in Madrid, the city was beautiful, and it was a fantastic trip.

summary.takeaway: Imperfect = inside the ongoing scene (era, estaba, hablaba); Preterite = the completed event or final verdict (hablé, comí, fue).

title: desde hace & Present Duration
subtitle: vivo aquí desde hace tres años — using present tense for actions that continue

use_example.german: Vivo en Madrid desde hace tres años y estoy aquí desde el lunes.
use_example.english: I have lived in Madrid for three years and I have been here since Monday.

summary.takeaway: If the action is still happening right now, keep the verb in the present tense and add desde (since point) or desde hace (for duration).

title: desde vs desde hace
subtitle: Starting point (desde el lunes) vs elapsed duration (desde hace tres años) with the present tense

use_example.german: Estamos aquí desde el lunes y vivo en Madrid desde hace dos años.
use_example.english: We have been here since Monday and I have lived in Madrid for two years.

summary.takeaway: desde + point in time ('since'); desde hace + quantity of time ('for').

title: Llevar + Time Expressions
subtitle: llevar tres años aquí: Spanish's ultra-natural 'carry time' idiom for ongoing duration

use_example.german: Vivo en esta ciudad desde hace diez años.
use_example.english: I have lived in this city for ten years.

summary.takeaway: Spanish views ongoing duration as present reality (vivo / estoy / llevo).

title: Comparatives: más, menos, mejor
subtitle: más... que, menos... que, tan... como, and irregular mejor/peor

use_example.german: Madrid es más grande que Toledo y este café es mejor que ese.
use_example.english: Madrid is bigger than Toledo and this coffee is better than that one.

summary.takeaway: más/menos/mejor/peor close with que ('than'); tan closes with como ('as').

title: Superiority and Inferiority
subtitle: más grande que, menos caro que, and superlatives el/la más grande

use_example.german: Este hotel es más económico que ese y esta es la ciudad más hermosa.
use_example.english: This hotel is more economical than that one and this is the most beautiful city.

summary.takeaway: el/la + noun + más [adj] = 'the most [adj] / the [adj]-est'.

title: Equality and Irregulars
subtitle: tan... como ('as... as'), mejor ('better/best'), and peor ('worse/worst')

use_example.german: Es mi mejor amigo y este es el mejor restaurante de la ciudad.
use_example.english: He is my best friend and this is the best restaurant in the city.

summary.takeaway: After a superlative ('the best restaurant IN the city'), Spanish always uses de ('of the city').

title: Double Object Pronouns
subtitle: me lo da, te lo digo — pronouns stacking before the verb, and le lo becoming se lo

use_example.german: Te lo digo hoy y se lo doy mañana.
use_example.english: I tell it to you today and I give it to him/her tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: People before things (me lo, te lo, nos lo) — and whenever le/les meets lo/la, it becomes se lo / se la!

title: The Pronoun Highway Order
subtitle: People before things: Indirect object (me, te, nos) precedes direct object (lo, la): me lo da, te lo digo

use_example.german: Te digo la verdad — sí, te la digo ahora.
use_example.english: I tell you the truth — yes, I tell it to you now.

summary.takeaway: Always keep the sequence: [no] + [indirect person] + [direct thing] + [verb].

title: The se lo Softening Rule
subtitle: Why *le lo sounds like a tongue-twister and becomes se lo (Se lo doy 'I give it to him/her')

use_example.german: Tengo la confirmación y se la voy a dar hoy.
use_example.english: I have the confirmation and I am going to give it to him/her today.

summary.takeaway: Whenever le or les meets lo, la, los, or las, it transforms into se.

title: Direct vs Indirect Objects: lo/la vs le
subtitle: lo/la (accusative) vs le/les (dative) — clarifying target and recipient

use_example.german: Veo a María y le doy el libro.
use_example.english: I see María and I give her the book.

summary.takeaway: Specific people as direct objects wear the personal 'a' (Veo a mi amigo) — and indirect recipients take le/les.

title: The Personal 'a'
subtitle: Placing 'a' before specific human direct objects: veo a María, conozco a tu hermano, invito a mi amigo

use_example.german: Visito Madrid y voy a visitar a mis padres.
use_example.english: I visit Madrid and I am going to visit my parents.

summary.takeaway: If the direct object is a specific person, put 'a' in front of them.

title: Dative Pronoun Redundancy
subtitle: Why Spanish loves saying 'to whom' twice: Le doy el libro a María, A mí me gusta

use_example.german: Le doy la llave a mi madre y le explico la situación a mi amigo.
use_example.english: I give the key to my mother and I explain the situation to my friend.

summary.takeaway: In Spanish, 'a [person]' (recipient) and pre-verbal le/les work as a team rather than an either/or choice.

title: Saber vs Conocer
subtitle: Knowing facts and skills (sé nadar, sé dónde está) vs knowing people and places (conozco Madrid, conozco a María)

use_example.german: Conozco Madrid, conozco a tu amigo y sé dónde está el restaurante.
use_example.english: I know Madrid, I know your friend, and I know where the restaurant is.

summary.takeaway: Facts, clauses, and infinitives take saber (sé); people and places take conocer (conozco).

title: Reflexives & Daily Life
subtitle: me llamo, levantarse, acostarse — reflexives as self-action and daily routine

use_example.german: Me levanto a las siete y nos vemos mañana.
use_example.english: I get up at seven and we'll see each other tomorrow.

summary.takeaway: Without me/te/se/nos, you lift or lay someone else; with me/te/se/nos, you get up and go to bed yourself!

title: Morning to Night Routine
subtitle: levantarse (me levanto), lavarse, vestirse, acostarse (me acuesto) across a full day

use_example.german: Me levanto a las siete de la mañana y quiero acostarme a las diez.
use_example.english: I get up at seven in the morning and I want to go to bed at ten.

summary.takeaway: With a clock hour, 'in the morning / at night' uses de (a las siete de la mañana); without a clock hour, it uses por (por la mañana)!

title: Non-Literal & Reciprocal Reflexives
subtitle: irse ('to leave'), quedarse ('to stay'), and nos vemos ('we see each other')

use_example.german: Me voy ahora — ¡nos vemos el viernes!
use_example.english: I'm leaving now — see you on Friday!

summary.takeaway: voy = 'I go [somewhere]'; me voy = 'I'm leaving!'

title: Gustar: The Inverted Liking
subtitle: me gusta el café = coffee pleases me — the subject is the thing liked

use_example.german: Me gusta la música y me gustan mucho los libros.
use_example.english: I like music and I like books very much.

summary.takeaway: The thing liked is the subject: singular/infinitive = gusta; plural noun = gustan!

title: gusta vs gustan
subtitle: Singular vs plural agreement: me gusta el café / me gusta viajar vs me gustan los libros

use_example.german: Me gusta visitar Madrid y me gustan mucho los restaurantes.
use_example.english: I like visiting Madrid and I like the restaurants very much.

summary.takeaway: Infinitives always take singular gusta (Me gusta comer); plural nouns take gustan (Me gustan los libros).

title: The Gustar Family
subtitle: encantar (me encanta), interesar (me interesa), importar (no me importa), doler (me duele la cabeza)

use_example.german: Me encanta la música, me encantan los libros y hoy me duele la cabeza.
use_example.english: I love music, I love books, and today my head hurts.

summary.takeaway: With body parts (Me duele la cabeza), Spanish uses me/te/le + the definite article (la cabeza) rather than mi/tu/su!

title: The Would-World & Subjunctive Preview
subtitle: me gustaría, podrías, and the opposite-vowel subjunctive after wishes

use_example.german: Me gustaría reservar una mesa y quiero que hables con mi amigo.
use_example.english: I would like to reserve a table and I want you to speak with my friend.

summary.takeaway: Conditional = infinitive + -ía; Subjunctive = flip -ar to -e and -er/-ir to -a after que.

title: The Conditional of Politeness
subtitle: Infinitive + -ía: me gustaría reservar, ¿podrías ayudarme?, sería fantástico

use_example.german: Me gustaría reservar una mesa para dos — ¿podrías confirmar?
use_example.english: I would like to reserve a table for two — could you confirm?

summary.takeaway: Infinitive + -ía = 'would [verb]'.

title: Triggering the Subjunctive
subtitle: The opposite-vowel switch (-ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a) after quiero que and es importante que

use_example.german: Quiero que hables con mi padre y es importante que tengas el billete.
use_example.english: I want you to speak with my father and it is important that you have the ticket.

summary.takeaway: Yo form minus -o + opposite vowel (-ar → -e, -er/-ir → -a) gives you the subjunctive!

title: Ojalá & W.E.I.R.D.O. Triggers
subtitle: Arabic-heritage ojalá ('God willing / hopefully') and wishes, emotions, and doubts in the subjunctive

use_example.german: ¡Ojalá tengas tiempo mañana — es bueno que tengas la llave!
use_example.english: I hope you have time tomorrow — it is good that you have the key!

summary.takeaway: Whenever you say ojalá ('hopefully / I hope'), flip the verb into the subjunctive!

title: The Silent H & Palatal Shifts
subtitle: Historical sound shifts: f- → h- (hacer, hijo, hierro, hambre, hermoso), -ct- → -ch- (noche, leche, ocho, hecho), pl-/cl- → ll- (llave, lluvia, lleno, llamar)

use_example.german: Tengo la llave de hierro y el restaurante está lleno esta noche.
use_example.english: I have the iron key and the restaurant is full tonight.

summary.takeaway: When you see initial silent h-, think f-; when you see -ch-, think -ct-; when you see ll-, think pl-/cl-!

title: The Silent H Decoded
subtitle: hacer ↔ fact, hijo ↔ filial, hierro ↔ ferrous, hambre ↔ famine, hermoso ↔ formosa: seeing Latin F behind Spanish H

use_example.german: Mi hijo quiere hacer una reservación en esta ciudad hermosa.
use_example.english: My son wants to make a reservation in this beautiful city.

summary.takeaway: Spanish hacer covers both English 'do' and 'make'.

title: The Palatal Twins: -ch- & ll-
subtitle: noctem → noche, lactem → leche, factum → hecho (-ct- → -ch-) and clāvis → llave, plēnus → lleno (cl-/pl- → ll-)

use_example.german: Esta noche el hotel está lleno por la lluvia, pero tengo mi llave.
use_example.english: Tonight the hotel is full because of the rain, but I have my key.

summary.takeaway: -ch- hides Latin -ct- (noche, leche, ocho, hecho); ll- hides Latin cl-/pl- (llave, lluvia, lleno, llamar).

title: que & quien: Connective Tissue
subtitle: Relative pronouns connecting ideas: la persona que conozco, lo que quiero

use_example.german: Es el libro que quiero y comprendo perfectamente lo que dices.
use_example.english: It is the book that I want and I understand perfectly what you are saying.

summary.takeaway: Never drop 'que' in Spanish — and translate non-question 'what' ('the thing that') as lo que!

title: que as the Master Connector
subtitle: Why Spanish uses que for BOTH people and things (el hombre que habla, el café que quiero), never dropping 'that'

use_example.german: El amigo que vive aquí tiene el libro que quiero.
use_example.english: The friend who lives here has the book that I want.

summary.takeaway: Whether the noun is a person ('who') or a thing ('that/which'), reach for que.

title: lo que: The Thing That / What
subtitle: Using neuter lo que for 'what / the thing that': Comprendo lo que dices, Lo que quiero es descansar

use_example.german: Comprendo lo que dices y sé lo que quiero.
use_example.english: I understand what you say and I know what I want.

summary.takeaway: Whenever English 'what' can be rephrased as 'the thing that', Spanish says lo que.

title: Verb Dynasties: poner, tener, traer & mostrar Matrices
subtitle: Language Transfer's Latin prefix × root matrix: suponer/proponer/componer, obtener/mantener, atraer/distraer, mostrar/demostrar

use_example.german: Supongo que quieres mantener la tradición y obtener la confirmación.
use_example.english: I suppose that you want to maintain the tradition and obtain the confirmation.

summary.takeaway: English -pose = Spanish -poner (pongo); English -tain = Spanish -tener (tengo); English -tract = Spanish -traer (traigo)!

title: Spanish Idioms as Thought
subtitle: tener ganas de, darse cuenta de, echar de menos, ojalá — cultural metaphors in everyday speech

use_example.german: Tienes razón — de hecho, tengo mucha hambre hoy.
use_example.english: You are right — in fact, I am very hungry today.

summary.takeaway: de hecho / en realidad = 'actually'; actualmente = 'currently'; darse cuenta = 'to realize'.

title: Everyday Idioms in Action
subtitle: tener ganas de ('to feel like'), darse cuenta de ('to realize'), de repente ('suddenly')

use_example.german: Tienes razón — ¿me traes la cuenta, por favor?
use_example.english: You are right — will you bring me the bill, please?

summary.takeaway: la cuenta = 'the bill/check'; traer = 'to bring'.

title: Arabic Heritage & Cultural Turns
subtitle: ojalá ('inshallah'), hasta ('hatta'), azul ('lazaward'), and la sobremesa

use_example.german: ¡Adiós, hasta mañana — ojalá tengas un buen día!
use_example.english: Goodbye, until tomorrow — I hope you have a great day!

summary.takeaway: Spanish is a tapestry of Latin structure and rich historical layers including Arabic and Greek.

title: Capstone: El Puente Reading
subtitle: One connected Madrid story synthesizing all 9 conversion bridges and key structures

use_example.german: Me encanta esta ciudad mágica, comprendo perfectamente lo que dices y se lo voy a explicar a mi amigo.
use_example.english: I love this magical city, I understand perfectly what you say, and I am going to explain it to my friend.

summary.takeaway: You don't memorize Spanish — you reconstruct it live from the Latin and structural bridges you already own.

title: A Day in Madrid: Reading
subtitle: Connected narrative in Madrid combining ser/estar, preterite/imperfect, gustar, and object pronouns

use_example.german: El día era hermoso, el café estaba caliente y ayer fue un día mágico en Madrid.
use_example.english: The day was beautiful, the coffee was hot, and yesterday was a magical day in Madrid.

summary.takeaway: era = ongoing trait; estaba = ongoing state/location; fue = completed event verdict.

title: Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild
subtitle: Mastering all 18 false friends (actualmente, embarazada, librería, éxito, asistir, recordar, sensible, sopa, realizar, lectura, delito, compromiso)

use_example.german: Actualmente vivo en Madrid, quiero asistir a la reunión y comprar un libro en la librería.
use_example.english: Currently I live in Madrid, I want to attend the meeting, and buy a book at the bookstore.

summary.takeaway: Always pause on actualmente (currently), librería (bookstore), éxito (success), asistir (attend), recordar (remember), and embarazada (pregnant).

title: The Whole-Trail Review Game
subtitle: Mixed-mode synthesis across all 30 topics of El Puente

use_example.german: Conozco Madrid, comprendo perfectamente lo que dices y ojalá tengas tiempo para celebrar.
use_example.english: I know Madrid, I understand perfectly what you say, and I hope you have time to celebrate.

summary.takeaway: You now own the structural engine of Spanish — every new word you hear will snap into this framework.

title: ¡Hola! y Gracias
subtitle: Greetings, thanks and politeness in dialogue drills; social warmth culture

use_example.german: ¡Hola! Un café, por favor. — Muchas gracias.
use_example.english: Hello! A coffee, please. — Thank you very much.

summary.takeaway: gracias is feminine plural ('graces'), so 'thank you very much' is muchas gracias.

title: The Alphabet & Me llamo
subtitle: El alfabeto, spelling your name, me llamo — introducing yourself with taught pieces

use_example.german: ¡Buenos días! Me llamo Alex — ¿cómo te llamas?
use_example.english: Good morning! My name is Alex — what is your name?

summary.takeaway: me llamo is literally 'I call myself' (from llamar, Latin clāmāre).

title: The Five Pure Vowels
subtitle: Never glide into diphthongs: clean vowel training and acute accent rules

use_example.german: Quiero café con leche y el agua, por favor.
use_example.english: I want coffee with milk and the water, please.

summary.takeaway: Spanish vowels never glide — and feminine nouns starting with stressed /a/ borrow el in the singular (el agua).

title: Actualmente, Librería & Co.
subtitle: Key false friends in contrastive recall drills: actualmente, librería, éxito, asistir, recordar, sensible, sopa, embarazada

use_example.german: Quiero recordar el momento porque la reservación es un éxito.
use_example.english: I want to remember the moment because the reservation is a success.

summary.takeaway: actualmente = currently; librería = bookstore; éxito = success; asistir = attend; recordar = remember; embarazada = pregnant.

title: The Social Line
subtitle: Register decisions with tú, usted, and ustedes across Spain and Latin America

use_example.german: ¿Cómo está usted, señor, y cómo están ustedes?
use_example.english: How are you, sir, and how are you all?

summary.takeaway: usted takes the 3rd-person singular verb; ustedes takes the 3rd-person plural verb (-n) across the entire Hispanic world.

title: Directions & Places
subtitle: Asking ¿Dónde está…? and navigating with todo recto, a la izquierda, a la derecha, aquí, allí

use_example.german: ¿Dónde está la estación y hay un restaurante bueno por aquí?
use_example.english: Where is the station and is there a good restaurant around here?

summary.takeaway: el/la (the specific place) → está; un/una (a place) → hay.

title: ¿Cuánto es?
subtitle: Asking prices with ¿Cuánto cuesta? / ¿Cuánto es?, numbers 1–100, and pedir la cuenta

use_example.german: ¿Cuánto es esto? — Son veinte euros, por favor.
use_example.english: How much is this? — It is twenty euros, please.

summary.takeaway: Plural prices use Son ('Son diez euros') — and prices in exchange always take por.

title: No he terminado
subtitle: Keeping haber and its participle glued together: No he terminado, ¿Ya has comido?, Nunca he visto

use_example.german: No he terminado hoy y no lo he visto.
use_example.english: I haven't finished today and I haven't seen it.

summary.takeaway: Think of he visto / he hablado / hemos hecho as a single compound word — nothing can step inside it.

title: De la mañana a la noche
subtitle: Chaining reflexives (me levanto, me lavo, me acuesto) and time markers across a realistic day

use_example.german: Por la mañana me levanto a las siete y por la noche me acuesto a las diez.
use_example.english: In the morning I get up at seven and at night I go to bed at ten.

summary.takeaway: empezar (e→ie) always takes 'a' before a following infinitive: Empiezo a comprender.

title: Relative Clauses in Depth
subtitle: que, quien (after prepositions: la persona con quien hablo), lo que, and donde

use_example.german: Es el amigo con quien hablé ayer en la ciudad donde vivo.
use_example.english: He is the friend with whom I spoke yesterday in the city where I live.

summary.takeaway: Keep prepositions right in front of quien (con quien, para quien) — never at the end of the sentence!

title: Hypothetical Situations
subtitle: Conditional -ía across verbs and polite/hypothetical expressions

use_example.german: Me gustaría vivir en esta ciudad hermosa y compraría una casa aquí.
use_example.english: I would like to live in this beautiful city and I would buy a house here.

summary.takeaway: Even two-letter ir ('to go') forms its conditional regularly: ir + -ía = iría ('would go')!

title: o→ue & e→ie: puedo, duermo, empiezo
subtitle: Why the vowel splits inside the singular and 3rd-person plural boot, and stays single in nosotros

use_example.german: Prefiero el café por la mañana y duermo ocho horas por la noche.
use_example.english: I prefer coffee in the morning and I sleep eight hours at night.

summary.takeaway: Follow your voice stress: stressed stem splits (ie/ue); stressed ending (-amos/-emos/-imos) stays single.

title: e→i & -go Verbs: pido, digo, hago, pongo
subtitle: Ordering with pido, telling with digo, doing with hago, and putting with pongo

use_example.german: Pido un café, digo la verdad y pongo la llave en la mesa.
use_example.english: I order a coffee, I tell the truth, and I put the key on the table.

summary.takeaway: Learn the five -go verbs together: tengo, hago, pongo, digo, traigo.

title: En el Restaurante: La Mesa & La Cuenta
subtitle: Reserving una mesa, ordering with quiero / para mí, and asking for la cuenta

use_example.german: Buenas tardes, quiero reservar una mesa para dos, por favor.
use_example.english: Good afternoon, I want to reserve a table for two, please.

summary.takeaway: una mesa para dos ('a table for two'), para mí ('for me'), and ¿me trae la cuenta? ('will you bring me the bill?').

title: Pan, Queso, Vino & El Agua Fría
subtitle: Table staples and why feminine agua and hambre take masculine el in the singular (el agua fría)

use_example.german: El agua está fría y la sopa está caliente y muy rica.
use_example.english: The water is cold and the soup is hot and very delicious.

summary.takeaway: el agua wears masculine el in front, but takes feminine adjectives after it: el agua fría!

title: La Estación, El Tren & El Billete
subtitle: Navigating la estación, el tren, el billete, and departure times

use_example.german: ¿Dónde está la estación de tren? Tengo un billete para Madrid.
use_example.english: Where is the train station? I have a ticket for Madrid.

summary.takeaway: Noun +noun compounds in Spanish link with de: el billete de tren ('the train ticket'), la estación de tren ('the train station').

title: Ida y Vuelta, Salida & Llegada
subtitle: Buying one-way (sencillo / de ida) and round-trip (de ida y vuelta) tickets with para + city

use_example.german: Quiero dos billetes para Madrid mañana en tren, por favor.
use_example.english: I want two tickets for Madrid tomorrow by train, please.

summary.takeaway: Travel by a vehicle takes en without an article: en tren ('by train').

title: Médico, Profesor & Actor (No 'un'!)
subtitle: Why Spanish drops un/una after ser before unmodified professions: Soy profesor, Ella es doctora

use_example.german: Soy profesor en la universidad y mi madre es una doctora muy buena.
use_example.english: I am a teacher at the university and my mother is a very good doctor.

summary.takeaway: Soy profesor (bare identity = no un) vs Es un profesor excelente (with adjective = un returns).

title: La Música, El Cine & Los Libros
subtitle: Talking about music, cinema, and books with me gusta / me encanta + definite article

use_example.german: Me encanta la música clásica, me gustan los libros y vamos al cine esta noche.
use_example.english: I love classical music, I like books, and we're going to the movies tonight.

summary.takeaway: Never drop el/la/los/las when naming things you like after gustar or encantar!

title: La Cabeza, La Mano & El Corazón
subtitle: Why la mano is feminine despite -o, and expressing aches with me duele la cabeza

use_example.german: Me duele la cabeza hoy y tengo las manos frías.
use_example.english: My head hurts today and my hands are cold.

summary.takeaway: el día and el problema are masculine in -a; la mano is feminine in -o!

title: El Abrigo, El Vestido & Los Colores
subtitle: Describing clothing with llevar ('to wear/carry') and post-nominal color agreement

use_example.german: Quiero comprar este abrigo negro y ese vestido rojo.
use_example.english: I want to buy this black coat and that red dress.

summary.takeaway: Notice that el vestido ('the dress') ends in -o and is grammatically masculine: un vestido rojo!
